prompt:
A *tangent line* to a circle is a line that intersects the circle in exactly one point. A *common tangent line* to two circles is a line that is tangent to both circles. As an example, in the figure, line $a$ is a common tangent to both circles, but line $b$ is only tangent to the larger circle.

Given two distinct circles in the plane, let $n$ be the number of common tangent lines that can be drawn to these two circles. What are all possible values of $n$? Your answer should include drawings with explanations.
answer: $n\in\{0,1,2,3,4\}$: one circle inside the other ($0$), internally tangent ($1$), crossing at two points ($2$), externally tangent ($3$), separate and outside each other ($4$).

solutions.title: Go through the relative positions
solutions.body:
Let the circles have centers $O_1,O_2$ and radii $r_1\ge r_2$, and let $d=O_1O_2$. (If $d=0$ and $r_1=r_2$, the circles would be equal, so this does not happen.) Every common tangent touches each circle at one point and has each circle entirely on one side. It is either *external* (both circles on the same side) or *internal* (the circles on opposite sides, so the line passes between them).

- **$n=0$: one circle strictly inside the other** ($d<r_1-r_2$). Any line tangent to the inner circle passes through an interior point of the outer circle, so it cuts the outer circle in two points. No common tangents.
- **$n=1$: internally tangent** ($d=r_1-r_2>0$). The tangent line at the point of contact touches both circles. Any other tangent line of the small circle passes inside the big circle, as in the previous case. Exactly $1$.
- **$n=2$: crossing at two points** ($r_1-r_2<d<r_1+r_2$). No line can pass between the circles, since they overlap, so there are no internal tangents. There are two external tangents, one on each side of the line of centers. Exactly $2$.
- **$n=3$: externally tangent** ($d=r_1+r_2$). The two external tangents, plus the common tangent at the point of contact, which separates the circles. Exactly $3$.
- **$n=4$: separate, neither inside the other** ($d>r_1+r_2$). Two external tangents and two internal tangents, the latter crossing between the circles. Exactly $4$.

These cases cover every pair of distinct circles. (Draw one picture for each case: a small circle inside a big one; a small circle touching a big one from inside; two overlapping circles with the two tangents along the "outside"; two touching circles with three tangents; two separate circles with four tangents forming an X between them.)

**Answer: $n$ can be $0, 1, 2, 3$, or $4$.**

prompt:
Ara and Bea play a game where they take turns putting numbers from $1$ to $5$ into the cells of the X-shaped diagram shown. Each number must be played exactly once, and a cell cannot have more than one number placed in it. Ara's goal is for the two diagonals of the X diagram to have the same sum when the game is over; Bea's goal is for these two sums to be unequal.

(a) Show that Ara can always win if he goes first.

(b) Show that Bea can always win if she goes first.
answer: (a) Ara puts $5$ in the center, then answers Bea's $n$ in a corner with $5-n$ in the opposite corner; both diagonals then sum to $10$. (b) Bea puts $2$ in the center; the two diagonal sums then total $17$, which is odd, so they cannot be equal.

solutions.title: Control the center
solutions.body:
The center cell lies on both diagonals and the four corners each lie on one. So at the end,
$$(\text{sum of diagonal 1})+(\text{sum of diagonal 2})=(1+2+3+4+5)+(\text{center})=15+(\text{center}).$$

**(a)** Ara first places $5$ in the center. Then the two diagonal sums will total $15+5=20$. Bea must now put some number $n\in\{1,2,3,4\}$ in a corner. Ara answers with $5-n$ in the opposite corner of the same diagonal. This is possible because $5-n$ is also in $\{1,2,3,4\}$ and $5-n\ne n$ (as $n\ne\tfrac52$), so it has not been used yet, and the opposite corner is empty. That diagonal now has sum $5+n+(5-n)=10$. Whatever happens with the last two numbers, the other diagonal has sum $20-10=10$ too. Ara wins.

**(b)** Bea first places $2$ in the center. The two diagonal sums will total $15+2=17$, an odd number. Two equal integers have an even total, so the sums can never be equal, whatever the remaining moves. Bea wins. (Placing $4$ in the center also works.) ∎

prompt:
Mr. Murgatroyd decides to throw his class a pizza party, but he's going to make them hunt for it first. He chooses eleven locations in the school, which we'll call $1, 2, \dots, 11$. His plan is to tell students to start at location $1$, and at each location $n$ from $1$ to $10$, they will find a message directing them to go to location $n+1$; at location $11$, there's pizza!

Mr. Murgatroyd sends his teaching assistant to post the ten messages in locations $1$ to $10$. Unfortunately, the assistant jumbles up the message cards at random before posting them. If the students begin at location $1$ as planned and follow the directions at each location, show that they will still get to the pizza.
answer: Each of the locations $2,\dots,11$ is named on exactly one message and location $1$ on none. So the students can never return to a location they have already visited (the first repeat would have to be location $1$), and they must reach $11$ within $10$ moves.

solutions.title: No location can be entered twice
solutions.body:
The ten messages say "go to $2$", "go to $3$", …, "go to $11$", one of each, posted in locations $1$ through $10$. So **each of the locations $2,\dots,11$ is the target of exactly one message, and location $1$ is the target of none.**

Let the locations visited be $v_0=1, v_1, v_2,\dots$, where each $v_{m}$ ($m\ge1$) is the target of the message at $v_{m-1}$. Suppose some location is visited twice, and pick the repeat $v_i=v_j$ ($i<j$) with $j$ as small as possible.

- If $i=0$, then $v_j=1$ is the target of a message, which is impossible.
- If $i\ge1$, then $v_i=v_j$ is the target of the messages at $v_{i-1}$ and at $v_{j-1}$. Only one message points to this location, and it hangs in one place, so $v_{i-1}=v_{j-1}$. That is an earlier repeat (since $j-1<j$), which contradicts the choice of $j$.

So the students never visit any location twice. There are only $11$ locations, so after at most $10$ moves the walk must end, and it can only end at location $11$, where there is no message. They get to the pizza. ∎

prompt:
Given a positive integer $N$ (written in base $10$), define its *integer substrings* to be integers that are equal to strings of one or more consecutive digits from $N$, including $N$ itself. For example, the integer substrings of $3208$ are $3$, $2$, $0$, $8$, $32$, $20$, $320$, $208$, and $3208$. (The substring $08$ is omitted from this list because it is the same integer as the substring $8$, which is already listed.)

What is the greatest integer $N$ such that no integer substring of $N$ is a multiple of $9$? (Note: $0$ is a multiple of $9$.)

solutions.title: Prefix sums and the pigeonhole principle
solutions.body:
Recall that an integer is divisible by $9$ exactly when its digit sum is. (Reason: $10^k-1=99\dots9$ is a multiple of $9$, so $\overline{d_k\dots d_1d_0}=\sum d_i10^i$ differs from $\sum d_i$ by a multiple of $9$.)

**$88{,}888{,}888$ works.** Its integer substrings are made of $k$ eights ($1\le k\le8$), with digit sum $8k$, and $9\nmid 8k$ for $1\le k\le 8$.

**Every larger $N$ fails.** If $N>88{,}888{,}888$ has $8$ digits, one of its digits is $9$, and that single digit is a substring divisible by $9$. Otherwise $N$ has at least $9$ digits. Let $s_0=0$ and let $s_k$ be the sum of the first $k$ digits of $N$, for $k=1,\dots,9$. These are $10$ numbers, but there are only $9$ possible remainders mod $9$. So by the pigeonhole principle, $s_j\equiv s_k\pmod 9$ for some $j<k$. Then $s_k-s_j$, the digit sum of the block of digits in positions $j+1,\dots,k$, is a multiple of $9$, so that block is an integer substring divisible by $9$. (If the block starts with zeros it is still a multiple of $9$, possibly $0$.)

**Answer: $88{,}888{,}888$**

prompt: In the following figure—not drawn to scale!—$E$ is the midpoint of $BC$, triangle $FEC$ has area $7$, and quadrilateral $DBEG$ has area $27$. Triangles $ADG$ and $GEF$ have the same area, $x$. Find $x$.

solutions.title: Chase areas with equal bases
solutions.body:
Write $[\,\cdot\,]$ for area. In the figure, $D$ is on $AB$, $G=AE\cap DC$, and $F$ is on $GC$.

1. Draw $GB$. Triangles $GBE$ and $GEC$ have equal bases $BE=EC$ and the same height from $G$, so $[GBE]=[GEC]=x+7$. Then $[GDB]=[DBEG]-[GBE]=27-(x+7)=20-x$.
2. Draw $AC$. Triangles $ABE$ and $AEC$ have equal bases and the same height from $A$, and $[ABE]=[ADG]+[DBEG]=x+27$. So $[AEC]=x+27$, $[AGC]=[AEC]-[GEC]=20$, and $[CAD]=[AGC]+[ADG]=20+x$. Also $[CDB]=[DBEG]+[GEC]=34+x$.
3. Triangles $GAD$ and $GDB$ share the height from $G$ to line $AB$, so $\dfrac{AD}{DB}=\dfrac{x}{20-x}$. Triangles $CAD$ and $CDB$ share the height from $C$, so $\dfrac{AD}{DB}=\dfrac{20+x}{34+x}$.

Hence $x(34+x)=(20-x)(20+x)$, i.e. $2x^2+34x-400=0$, i.e. $x^2+17x-200=(x-8)(x+25)=0$. Since $x>0$, $x=8$.

**Answer: $x=8$**

In the following figure—not drawn to scale!—$E$ is the midpoint of $BC$, triangle $FEC$ has area $7$, and quadrilateral $DBEG$ has area $27$. Triangles $ADG$ and $GEF$ have the same area, $x$. Find $x$.

Zaineb makes a large necklace from beads labeled $290, 291, 292, \dots, 2023$. She uses each bead exactly once, arranging the beads in the necklace any order she likes. Prove that no matter how the beads are arranged, there must be three beads in a row whose labels are the side lengths of a triangle.
answer: There are $1734=6\cdot289$ beads. Cut the necklace into $578$ consecutive trios. If no trio formed a triangle, the sum $S$ of the two smaller labels of each trio would be at most the sum $T$ of the largest labels. But $S\ge 290+\dots+1445$ and $T\le 1446+\dots+2023$, and the first sum is larger.

solutions.title: Split into trios and compare sums
solutions.body:
We prove more generally: if $6n$ beads labeled $n+1,n+2,\dots,7n$ form a necklace, some three consecutive beads are the side lengths of a triangle. The problem is the case $n=289$: the labels $290,\dots,2023=7\cdot289$ are $1734=6\cdot289$ beads.

Three positive numbers $p\le q\le r$ are the sides of a (non-degenerate) triangle exactly when $p+q>r$. Suppose, for contradiction, that every three consecutive beads $p\le q\le r$ satisfy $p+q\le r$.

Starting anywhere, cut the necklace into $2n$ blocks of three consecutive beads. Let $S$ be the sum of the two smaller labels in all blocks ($4n$ labels), and $T$ the sum of the largest labels ($2n$ labels). Adding $p+q\le r$ over all blocks gives $S\le T$.

But $S$ is a sum of $4n$ different labels, so it is at least the sum of the $4n$ smallest labels:
$$S\ge (n+1)+(n+2)+\dots+5n=\frac{4n\,(6n+1)}{2}=12n^2+2n.$$
And $T$ is a sum of $2n$ different labels, so it is at most the sum of the $2n$ largest:
$$T\le (5n+1)+\dots+7n=\frac{2n\,(12n+1)}{2}=12n^2+n.$$
So $T\le 12n^2+n<12n^2+2n\le S$, which contradicts $S\le T$. Hence some three consecutive beads form a triangle. ∎

prompt: A *lattice point* in the plane is a point with integer coordinates. Let $T$ be a triangle in the plane whose vertices are lattice points, but with no other lattice points on its sides. Furthermore, suppose $T$ contains exactly four lattice points in its interior. Prove that these four points lie on a straight line.
answer: By Pick's theorem $[T]=\tfrac92$, so the edge vectors have determinant $\pm9\equiv0\pmod 3$. Working mod $3$, this forces the centroid $G$ to be a lattice point. Applying Pick's theorem again to $\triangle ABG$ (area $\tfrac32$) produces four collinear interior lattice points on a line through $G$.

solutions.title: Pick's theorem and arithmetic mod 3
solutions.body:
We use two standard facts.
- **Pick's theorem:** a lattice polygon with $i$ interior and $b$ boundary lattice points has area $i+\tfrac b2-1$.
- **Lattice points on a segment:** if $P,Q$ are lattice points and $g=\gcd$ of the coordinates of $Q-P$, the lattice points on segment $PQ$ are exactly $P+\tfrac{j}{g}(Q-P)$, $j=0,\dots,g$. They are equally spaced, and the same spacing continues along the whole line $PQ$.

Points are treated as vectors. A point $\alpha A+\beta B+\gamma C$ with $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=1$ is inside $\triangle ABC$ exactly when $\alpha,\beta,\gamma>0$.

**Step 1: the centroid is a lattice point.** Let $T=ABC$. By Pick, $[T]=4+\tfrac32-1=\tfrac92$. So with $u=B-A$, $v=C-A$, $\det(u,v)=\pm9\equiv0\pmod 3$. So $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent mod $3$.
- $u\not\equiv 0\pmod 3$: otherwise $A+\tfrac13u$ would be a lattice point on side $AB$. Likewise $v\not\equiv0$.
- So $v\equiv u$ or $v\equiv -u\pmod 3$. If $v\equiv u$, then $C-B=v-u\equiv 0$, and $B+\tfrac13(C-B)$ is a lattice point on side $BC$, which is impossible. So $u+v\equiv 0$, i.e. $A+B+C=3A+u+v\equiv 0\pmod 3$.

Hence $G=\tfrac13(A+B+C)$ is a lattice point, inside $T$.

**Step 2: look at $\triangle ABG$.** Its area is $\tfrac13[T]=\tfrac32$, and side $AB$ has no lattice points other than $A$ and $B$. Pick gives $\tfrac32=i'+\tfrac{b'}2-1$, i.e. $2i'+b'=5$ with $b'\ge3$. So either $(i',b')=(1,3)$ or $(0,5)$.

*Case $(1,3)$.* $\triangle ABG$ has no lattice points on its sides except its vertices and has area $\tfrac32$, so $\det(B-A,G-A)=\pm3\equiv0\pmod3$. Step 1 applies word for word to this triangle, so its centroid $G_1=\tfrac13(A+B+G)=\tfrac19(4A+4B+C)$ is a lattice point. Then the points $G_1+k(G-G_1)$, $k=0,1,2,3$, are lattice points on one line. Since $G-G_1=\tfrac19(2C-A-B)$, they are
$$\tfrac19\bigl((4-k)A+(4-k)B+(1+2k)C\bigr):\quad (4,4,1),\ (3,3,3),\ (2,2,5),\ (1,1,7)\ \text{(coefficients over 9)},$$
all with positive coefficients, so all four are inside $T$.

*Case $(0,5)$.* There are two lattice points on $AG\cup BG$ besides the vertices. By symmetry between $A$ and $B$, there are two subcases.
- One lattice point on each of $AG$ and $BG$. Then each is a midpoint, so the lattice points on line $AG$ are spaced $\tfrac12(G-A)$ apart. The next one beyond $G$ is $G+\tfrac12(G-A)=\tfrac12(3G-A)=\tfrac12(B+C)$, the midpoint of side $BC$. This is impossible.
- Two lattice points on $AG$ (its trisection points) and none on $BG$. Then the points $A+\tfrac j3(G-A)$ are lattice points for all integers $j$. Since $G-A=\tfrac13(B+C-2A)$, the ones with $j=1,2,3,4$ are
$$\tfrac19\bigl((9-2j)A+jB+jC\bigr):\quad (7,1,1),\ (5,2,2),\ (3,3,3),\ (1,4,4),$$
all inside $T$ and on one line.

In every possible case we found four collinear lattice points inside $T$. Since $T$ has exactly four interior lattice points, these are all of them, and they lie on a straight line. ∎
